<reason>Side A delivered an eloquent case centered on political economy and asymmetric risk, arguing that once private bottlers gain a stake in a municipal aquifer, they will lobby and litigate to delay drought cutoffs. However, Side B dismantled this route to victory in two ways. First, Side B directly answered Side A's pressure questions by specifying regulatory mechanisms—state-level telemetry triggers set at seasonal recharge baselines, "shut down first, litigate later" clauses, upfront surety bonds, and restricting royalties to capital pipe upgrades—that neutralize the risk of enforcement lag and budget dependency. Second, Side B trapped Side A in a fatal inconsistency regarding other industries: if governments are truly helpless against corporate litigation during a drought, Side A's exemption keeping agriculture and beverage manufacturing under "calibrated rules" would allow the exact same corporations to drain the exact same aquifers simply by adding sugar to make soda.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's dismantling in [B4.5] and [B5.1-B5.2] of Side A's distinction between water bottlers and soda/industrial plants ([A4.3]). Side B pointed out that soda is over 90% water—meaning a beverage plant cannot "alter inputs" away from water and faces the exact same sunk-cost incentive to fight pumping cutoffs—and that if water bottlers can relocate to non-municipal sources as Side A claimed in [A4.1], municipal extraction is no more their inescapable "core asset" than a soda plant's.</best_rebuttal>
